spans.content: ReviQ: A systematic literature review workbench
<sub>Philipp</sub> <sub>Haindl</sub> iD
University of Applied Sciences St. Pölten, Department of Computer Science & Security, St. Pölten, Austria
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Evidence-based software engineering
PRISMA
Reproducibility
Research methodology tool
Systematic literature review
A B S T R A C T
We present ReviQ, an open-source workbench for systematic literature reviews (SLRs) that runs locally in Docker
and does not require cloud accounts. The tool implements all eight phases of the Kitchenham and Charters (2007)
methodology: project setup, BibTeX import with cross-database deduplication, title/abstract screening, full-text
eligibility, snowballing with saturation tracking, quality assessment, configurable data extraction, and results
visualization, including PRISMA 2020 flow diagrams. Reviewer agreement is quantified through Cohen’s � with
asymptotic confidence intervals and PABAK, which is computed directly from the stored decisions. The complete
project state—decisions, conflict resolutions, QA scores, extraction records, taxonomies, and source BibTeX files—
can be exported as a versioned replication package and re-imported into another ReviQ instance, enabling third
parties to audit or continue a review. We validated ReviQ by conducting a complete SLR on a software engineering
topic across five databases, four snowballing iterations, 519 retrieved and 356 screened papers, involving two
reviewers and resulting in 40 included studies. ReviQ is released under the GPL v3 license
Current code version

platforms.

spans.content: 1 . Motivation and significance
The systematic literature review (SLR), as outlined by Kitchenham
and Charters [1] within the context of evidence-based software en-
gineering [2], comprises three main phases. Planning establishes the
research questions, the search strategy across the chosen databases, and
the inclusion/exclusion criteria. Conduct covers the execution of the
database searches and the processing of candidates through screening
by at least two independent reviewers, full-text eligibility assessment,
optional citation snowballing [3], quality assessment, and structured
data extraction. Reporting synthesises the extracted data and documents
the entire process—most prominently via a Preferred Reporting Items
for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [4,5] flow
diagram—so that the review can be audited and replicated. Each phase
generates artefacts—decision logs, conflict records, agreement statistics,
and PRISMA counts among them—which must be internally consistent
and accessible for replication.
Table 2

data extraction. Reporting synthesises the extracted data and documents
the entire process—most prominently via a Preferred Reporting Items
for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [4,5] flow
diagram—so that the review can be audited and replicated. Each phase
generates artefacts—decision logs, conflict records, agreement statistics,
and PRISMA counts among them—which must be internally consistent
and accessible for replication.
Since 2007, SLRs have become a widely adopted research method-
ology in the field of software engineering [6]. Subsequent work has
highlighted both their increasing utilization and the recurring method-
ological challenges associated with them [7,8]. A primary concern
in this context is the issue of tooling. When we conducted an SLR
on a JVM-related topic, we initially documented decisions using a
shared spreadsheet. It soon became evident that this approach was
inadequate—parallel edits resulted in merge conflicts, the � computa-
tion required re-derivation with each decision change, and the PRISMA
numbers in the manuscript frequently diverged from the actual counts
until discrepancies were identified. This experience, which appears to
be common among software engineering researchers [9,10], prompted
the development of ReviQ.
Numerous tools have been developed to address various aspects of
this issue. Marshall et al. [11] ofer a systematic feature analysis of ex-
isting SLR tools, while Al-Zubidy et al. [12] identify a prioritized set of
value-added requirements for SLR tooling infrastructure. Rayyan [13]
has emerged as the most widely adopted screening tool, featuring an
intuitive web interface with semi-automated duplicate detection and
label-based filtering; however, it is cloud-hosted and does not support
phases beyond screening. StArt [14] encompasses the entire systematic
reviewing process, including quality assessment (QA), and has recently
incorporated snowballing support; nonetheless, it does not compute
inter-rater agreement nor generate PRISMA 2020 diagrams. Parsifal<sup>1</sup>
provides a web-based, protocol-driven workflow with quality assessment
but lacks snowballing, � calculation, and any form of replication-
package export. Covidence<sup>2</sup> is extensively utilized in the health sciences
and ofers a refined dual-reviewer workflow with PRISMA output, yet it
is a commercial cloud product with a free tier limited to a single review.
Table 2 presents a comparison of features across these tools.
We developed ReviQ to address the existing gaps: a single, locally-
deployable application that encompasses all phases of the Kitchenham
and Charters methodology, calculates � with confidence intervals, gen-
erates PRISMA 2020 diagrams from live data, and consolidates the
entire project state into a portable replication package. The tool oper-
ates within Docker, stores all data in a local SQLite database, and does
not connect to any external servers.
Fig. 1. Two-container architecture of ReviQ. Container 1 serves the React fron-
tend via Nginx; Container 2 runs the FastAPI backend with a persisted SQLite
database. Both run on the researcher’s machine.
The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes
the architecture of ReviQ and its eight functional phases. Section 3 il
lustrates ReviQ on a real validation SLR involving five databases, four
snowballing iterations, and two independent reviewers. Section 4 dis-
cusses the tool’s research and educational impact, its positioning against
related tools, and current limitations. Section 5 concludes.
2 . Software description
2.1 . Software architecture
ReviQ is a Docker [15] application comprising two containers, as il-
lustrated in Fig. 1. The first container operates Nginx, which serves the
React single-page application and reverse-proxies /api/* requests to the
second container, a FastAPI [16] service implemented in Python 3.12.
All state data is maintained within a SQLite database on a desig-
nated Docker volume (reviq-db-data), ensuring data persistence across
container rebuilds. Initiating the application merely requires execut-
ing docker compose up --build; there is no necessity for configuring
accounts, application programming interface (API) keys, or external
databases.
The backend comprises ten route modules—one per SLR phase
plus cross-cutting concerns like kappa, export, and report—and
two service modules (bibtex_service for parsing and deduplication,
kappa_service for agreement statistics). The database schema is struc-
tured with 16 SQLModel [17] tables that align with the SLR process,
encompassing projects, reviewers, inclusion/exclusion/QA criteria, pa-
pers, reviewer decisions, final decisions, conflict logs, QA scores, ex-
traction fields and records, snowballing iterations, taxonomy entries,
database search strings, and paper–database links. The frontend operates
exclusively through the REST API, with React Query managing all data
retrieval and cache invalidation, thereby ensuring that the user interface
is promptly updated upon the recording of a decision.
2.2 . Software functionalities
ReviQ realises the SLR methodology as eight sequential phases that
map onto the three main phases introduced in Section 1: Phase 1 (project
setup) corresponds to Planning; Phases 2–7 (import, screening, eligi-
bility, snowballing, quality assessment, and data extraction) constitute
Conduct; and Phase 8 (results and PRISMA visualisation) constitutes
Reporting. Fig. 2 illustrates the eight-phase ReviQ workflow, highlighting

ReviQ realises the SLR methodology as eight sequential phases that
map onto the three main phases introduced in Section 1: Phase 1 (project
setup) corresponds to Planning; Phases 2–7 (import, screening, eligi-
bility, snowballing, quality assessment, and data extraction) constitute
Conduct; and Phase 8 (results and PRISMA visualisation) constitutes
Reporting. Fig. 2 illustrates the eight-phase ReviQ workflow, highlighting
which phases are dual-reviewer activities, the iterative snowballing
loop, and the final output phase. The sidebar of the application orga-
nizes these phases in the same sequential order. At the top of each phase
page, a statistics bar displays real-time counts (retrieved, unique, dupli-
cates, included, excluded, undecided), providing the reviewer with a
continuous sense of progress.
Fig. 2. Eight-phase SLR workflow following Kitchenham and Charters [1]. The
dashed arrow indicates that snowballing [3] feeds new candidates back into
screening.

loop, and the final output phase. The sidebar of the application orga-
nizes these phases in the same sequential order. At the top of each phase
page, a statistics bar displays real-time counts (retrieved, unique, dupli-
cates, included, excluded, undecided), providing the reviewer with a
continuous sense of progress.
Phase 1—Setup. The researcher initiates a project by establishing a
title, description, and the name of the lead researcher, and registers
up to five reviewers. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are delineated for
each phase (screening or full-text), with each criterion assigned a la-
bel (e.g., E3) and a concise, human-readable name that subsequently
appears in the exclusion breakdown of the PRISMA diagram. Quality
assessment criteria are configured with a maximum score of either 0.5
or 1.0. Taxonomy categories (e.g., “Research Type” with values such as
“Evaluation Research”, “Solution Proposal”, etc.) and custom extraction
fields (free text, number, boolean, dropdown) are also defined at this
stage. Finally, for each database, the researcher documents the search
string, filter settings, search date, and result count—this metadata is
directly incorporated into the generated protocol report.
Phase 2—Import. BibTeX files are uploaded for each database from
a directory on the host machine. ReviQ processes these files using
bibtexparser [18] and performs deduplication across databases in two
stages: initially based on the normalized Digital Object Identifier (DOI;
converted to lowercase and stripped of whitespace), followed by a com-
posite key of normalized title and normalized venue for entries lacking
a DOI. The normalization process removes punctuation and collapses
whitespace, thereby addressing minor formatting discrepancies between
databases (e.g., “Proc. ICSE” versus “Proceedings of ICSE”). Each iden-
tified duplicate is logged with the citekey of the retained original;
reviewers have the option to examine this log and override individual de-
cisions if the heuristic proves incorrect. Language detection via langid
flags non-English abstracts, facilitating the eficient application of ex-
clusion criterion E3. A many-to-many link table (PaperDatabaseLink)
records which databases identified each paper, enabling the calculation
of per-database precision and recall in Phase 7.
Phase 3—Screening. Each reviewer independently categorizes every
paper as Include (I), Exclude (E), or Uncertain (U), with the option
to select the governing criterion (e.g., E2—insuficient focus) and pro-
vide a free-text rationale. Papers are presented individually, displaying
their title, authors, year, venue, abstract, and source database; a fil-
ter bar at the top facilitates narrowing the list to undecided, included,
excluded, or uncertain items. Decisions are recorded per reviewer in
the ReviewerDecision table. The backend system compares decisions
between the two primary reviewers and identifies disagreements as con-
flicts. These conflicts are displayed in a dedicated conflict tab (Fig. 4),
where each conflict shows the paper title, both reviewers’ decisions with
their rationales side by side, and controls to resolve the conflict through
discussion or arbitration. The resolution method and an optional note
are documented in the ConflictLog table. Decisions can be exported as
a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file, allowing co-reviewers work-
ing on separate machines to exchange them via email or shared drives
and import them back; the source_file field on each imported decision
preserves provenance.
Fig. 3 presents the screening view of Phase 3, with the paper list,
per-paper decision badges, the total/undecided/included/excluded/un-
certain counters, and the filter bar used to narrow the list during the
review. Fig. 4 illustrates the conflict resolution view, displaying both
reviewers’ decisions for a disputed paper alongside their rationales and
the controls used to record the resolution.
Phase 4—Eligibility. The same decision-making process is applicable
to the full-text assessment, utilizing the inclusion and exclusion criteria
established in Phase 1. Articles may include a full-text URL for expedited
access or be marked as inaccessible if the full text cannot be obtained.
Phase 5—Snowballing. Forward and backward citation chasing is con-
ducted in accordance with Wohlin [3]. Each iteration is represented as a
distinct entity within the database. The researcher imports a new BibTeX
batch labeled snowballing:N (where � denotes the iteration number),
which subsequently undergoes the standard screening and eligibility
process. The iteration overview (Fig. 5) illustrates, for each iteration,
the number of candidates retrieved, decided, included after screening,
excluded, and those still undecided, along with a saturation indicator.
When an iteration results in zero new inclusions, the researcher may
designate it as saturated, indicating that the snowballing process has
reached convergence.
Phase 6—Quality assessment. In the evaluation process, included pa-
pers are assessed according to the QA criteria established in Phase 1.
Each criterion is assigned a score of 0, 0.5, or 1 by individual reviewers.
These scores are then normalized to a percentage and categorized as high
(≥ 75% by default), medium (≥ 50%), or low, with both thresholds being
adjustable for each project. A summary view provides an overview of
the score distribution across all papers; Fig. 6 shows this distribution for
the validation SLR.
Phase 7—Data extraction. The extraction schema delineated in Phase 1
accommodates four distinct field types: free text, numerical, boolean,
and dropdown with project-specific option lists. Taxonomy categories
furnish an additional structured classification layer. A card view enumer-
ates all papers, accompanied by a progress badge indicating the number
of fields completed; a table view ofers a spreadsheet-style overview of
all extraction records, which can be exported as comma-separated val-
ues (CSV). Fig. 7 illustrates the Research Type and Contribution Type
taxonomy distributions for the validation SLR.
Phase 8—Results. The output is organized into three tabs. The PRISMA
Flow tab presents a PRISMA 2020 [4] diagram as an inline SVG, featuring
two parallel streams (database search and snowballing) and exclusion
breakdowns per criterion. This diagram is available for download in both
colour and greyscale variants suitable for publication. The Charts tab
provides visualisations along four reporting dimensions and is deliber-
ately not limited to selection metrics. For selection, it shows per-database

3 . Illustrative example
We employed ReviQ to perform an SLR on the usage patterns of a
Java runtime interface. The review was conducted by two reviewers and
encompassed five databases searched in February 2026: Scopus (217),
IEEE Xplore (162), ACM DL (172), SpringerLink (56), and DBLP (1),
totalling 608 hits. After BibTeX export and import, 495 records were
available for deduplication; ReviQ identified and removed 139 dupli-
cates via DOI and normalized title/venue matching, leaving 356 unique
papers.
Six inclusion criteria were defined to capture papers describing the
technology under review, discussing its practical applications, address-
ing challenges, or utilizing documented frameworks built upon it. Eleven
exclusion criteria covered duplicates, insuficient focus, non-English
publications, theses, non-peer-reviewed work, and of-topic domains.
3.1 . Database stream
Of the 356 screened papers, 326 were excluded at the title/abstract
screening, leaving 30 papers for full-text assessment. Of these, 6 were
excluded at the full-text stage, yielding 24 included studies from the
database search.
3.2 . Snowballing stream
Four forward citation iterations were conducted following
Wohlin [3]. Iterations 1 through 3 retrieved 9, 8, and 4 candi-
dates, of which 7, 6, and 3 were included respectively. Iteration 4
retrieved 3 candidates but included none, confirming saturation. Of
the 24 candidates retrieved in total, 8 were excluded during screening;
the remaining 16 proceeded to full-text assessment, all of which were
included, yielding 16 additional studies. The two streams together
yielded a final corpus of 40 studies. Fig. 9 presents the PRISMA 2020
diagram generated by ReviQ from the live project data.
Cohen’s � for screening was 0.509 (95% CI [0.331, 0.687]; PABAK =
0.486), indicating moderate agreement per Landis and Koch [23]. At
full-text eligibility, both reviewers agreed on every paper (� = 1.0).

4 . Impact
From a research standpoint, ReviQ significantly reduces the barriers
to conducting methodologically rigorous systematic literature reviews.
The integrated � computation eliminates a step that researchers fre-
quently defer to a separate spreadsheet, often resulting in inconsistent
calculations—sometimes applied to an incorrect subset of papers, some-
times using a 2×2 matrix when a 3×3 matrix would be more appropriate,
and occasionally omitted altogether. The live updates of � and PABAK
as decisions are recorded facilitate continuous monitoring of agreement
throughout the review process, rather than solely at its conclusion.
The generation of the PRISMA diagram from the same database that
stores the decisions ensures that the numbers in the diagram are consis-
tent with the decision log [24]. This provides stronger assurance than a
manually drawn figure, as our pre-ReviQ experience demonstrated that
altering a single screening decision could inadvertently invalidate the
PRISMA counts in the manuscript, with discrepancies only becoming
apparent during a meticulous final review—if at all.
The replication-package export consolidates the entire project state
into a versioned ZIP archive, thereby supporting the reproducibility
requirements that several software engineering venues have begun to
mandate. When published alongside an SLR, this package enables other
researchers to verify reported counts against actual decisions, reuse the
extraction data for meta-analyses, or extend the review with additional
snowballing iterations.
The decision to run all processes locally was intentional. Researchers
at institutions with restrictive data policies—or those handling embar-
goed submissions—may be prohibited from uploading paper metadata to
a third-party cloud service. ReviQ does not contact any external server.
The Docker-based deployment ensures consistent behavior across Linux,
macOS, and Windows without necessitating the manual installation of
Python, Node.js, or any other runtime.
Beyond its primary research application, ReviQ can also serve as an
educational tool. By enforcing the Kitchenham and Charters phase struc-
ture and making each step explicit—criteria definition before screen-
ing, dual-reviewer decisions before conflict resolution, and QA scoring
before extraction—it provides students with a concrete, interactive
walkthrough of the SLR methodology.

Limitations. Several limitations remain. The asynchronous collabora-
tion model, which relies on JSON export/import, works well for teams
of two or three but does not scale for larger groups; a Git-based or shared-
filesystem sync layer is a planned enhancement. Currently, only BibTeX
is supported as an import format; incorporating RIS and CSV import
capabilities would enhance compatibility with databases that default
to alternative formats. ReviQ does not yet provide AI-assisted screen-
ing, although the decision data stored within ReviQ, including paper
metadata, reviewer labels, and rationales, could serve as training data
for active-learning rankers. The PRISMA diagram presently implements
only the two-stream layout as prescribed by the PRISMA 2020 statement
(databases + other methods); reviews with more complex identification
paths would require manual adjustments to the generated SVG. Lastly,
ReviQ does not currently enforce blinding between reviewers—both re-
viewers can view each other’s names, although they cannot access each
other’s decisions until they are exchanged.
5 . Conclusions
We have introduced ReviQ, an open-source SLR workbench that com-
prehensively addresses all eight phases of the Kitchenham and Charters
methodology within a locally-deployed web application. The primary
contributions of ReviQ, which extend beyond the capabilities of existing
tools, include: (i) integrated computation of Cohen’s � and PABAK with
confidence intervals, updated in real-time as decisions are made; (ii)
automatic generation of PRISMA 2020 diagrams with exclusion counts
per criterion, rendered as publication-ready SVGs; and (iii) a versioned
replication-package export that consolidates all project data for archival
purposes or transfer.
We validated the tool through application to a real SLR in the soft-
ware engineering domain. This review involved two reviewers, five
databases, 519 retrieved records, four snowballing iterations, and 40 in-
cluded studies. The moderate screening agreement
and the
resolution of 19 conflicts via the built-in user interface demonstrate the
tool’s capability to manage typical levels of disagreement encountered
in practice. The PRISMA diagram and a 22-page protocol report were
generated directly from the stored data, afirming that ReviQ can facili-
tate a review from initial setup to publication-ready outputs without the
need for external tools.
Future developments will focus on enabling real-time collaboration
between reviewer instances, supporting RIS/CSV import, incorporating
AI-assisted pre-screening, and implementing reviewer blinding.

and the
resolution of 19 conflicts via the built-in user interface demonstrate the
tool’s capability to manage typical levels of disagreement encountered
in practice. The PRISMA diagram and a 22-page protocol report were
generated directly from the stored data, afirming that ReviQ can facili-
tate a review from initial setup to publication-ready outputs without the
need for external tools.
Future developments will focus on enabling real-time collaboration
between reviewer instances, supporting RIS/CSV import, incorporating
AI-assisted pre-screening, and implementing reviewer blinding.
